title: CORSIA a decade in – what’s the picture on the ground?
summary: Airlines, developers, IATA, and Boeing on CORSIA’s First Phase: tripling supply, the hurdles behind authorisation, and how deals get done.
body_markdown:
A decade ago, member states of the United Nations International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) adopted the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, or CORSIA.


Following the scheme’s pilot phase (2021-2023), with no compensation requirements for participating airlines, the voluntary First Phase (2024-2026) of the scheme now represents a demand close to 200mn CORSIA Eligible Emission Units (CEEUs). After a slow start, with airlines struggling with jet fuel prices, the CORSIA market is now moving forward. Airlines have started buying CEEUs in meaningful volumes and have already retired over 1mn units for CORSIA compliance. With the First Phase compliance deadline approaching, all actors in the scheme are now moving quickly.


Our[recent webinar](https://abatable.com/webinars-events/obligation-turns-into-opportunity-corsia-a-decade-in) brought together representatives from every side of the CORSIA market. Speakers from Malaysia Aviation Group, IATA, GenZero, Boeing, and the project developer Bridge Carbon joined Abatable to share what they've learned so far after six years of the scheme’s operation. Here we summarise the conversation and answer your questions from the session.


> Watch the full webinar[here](https://abatable.com/webinars-events/obligation-turns-into-opportunity-corsia-a-decade-in) .


### First, a quick refresher


**‍** CORSIA, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, aims for carbon-neutral growth in international civil aviation to 2035. Airline’s emissions above a set baseline must be compensated for by buying and retiring CORSIA-Eligible Emissions Units (CEEUs). To qualify, a unit must come from a project registered with an approved carbon crediting standard, comply with ICAO’s criteria on eligibility, and carry a host country's Letter of Authorisation (LoA) indicating its use for CORSIA.


The LoA commits the government to ‘correspondingly adjust’ the unit, meaning the host country removes the reduction from its own national accounts under the Paris Agreement on climate change, so the unit is not double-counted. If units only have an LoA, they must also receive[insurance](https://abatable.com/blog/how-does-corsia-insurance-work) against their revocation. Units do not need insurance if the corresponding adjustment has already been applied.


Five themes stood out from our conversation:


## Supply is growing fast, from a low base


For almost two years, a single jurisdictional REDD+ programme in Guyana, registered with ART, was the only source for every CEEU available on the market. That changed this year. The supply of CEEUs moved from around 16.8mn tonnes in January to 54.4mn units by October, a threefold increase in nine months.


Several factors are behind the growth. A new wave of host countries have issued LoAs now that UNFCCC decisions on authorisation content and procedure under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement are settled. Some countries have already included LoAs and authorised units in their[first Biennial Transparency Report (BTR)](https://unfccc.int/first-biennial-transparency-reports) , a progress report under the Paris Agreement, confirming a corresponding adjustment and enabling unit tagging as CORSIA eligible. Insurers are innovating for the new market, offering cover against the risks of LoA revocation and of missing a corresponding adjustment of the authorised units. And airlines have become active in CORSIA compliance. Nine airlines have sourced and retired just over one million CEEUs over the last six months, giving developers a clear demand signal.


The gap between supply and demand is still wide. Abatable’s[analysis](https://abatable.com/blog/corsia-airlines-need-to-offset-58-mtco2) estimates First Phase demand, covering emissions from 2024 to 2026, at around 200mn units. That's more than the 160mn to 170mn credits buyers retire in the voluntary carbon market in a typical year. At $10 to $23 per tonne for CORSIA units, this represents a $2bn to $4.6bn market. The second phase, from 2027 to 2035, could need 1.2–1.8bn units, worth an estimated $12bn to $41bn.


Developers expect the shortfall to push prices up. Bridge Carbon reported that prices have recovered from the low $9s per tonne earlier this year to $12 to $13 by October. Traders have taken speculative positions in expectation of further rises as the January 2028 deadline nears.


## A Letter of Authorisation is only the first step


Much of the early CORSIA supply discussion focused on LoAs. Our panel made it clear that a letter starts a much longer process and that host-country readiness now sets the pace for new volumes.


As Minh Tran from Bridge Carbon outlined, their team assesses four things before committing to a new project. The first, and most important, is what it calls 'Article 6 readiness'. Does the host country have a national carbon framework that translates the Paris Agreement's rules into domestic law? Is its letter worded tightly enough to be contractually enforceable?


Developers also check whether the volume authorised is realistic when compared to the country's Paris Agreement climate pledge, or Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). A government that authorises too many credits may later revoke letters to protect its own climate target. And they ask whether it has the capacity to file its BTR on time, the step that makes the corresponding adjustment final.


The second factor is insurability. Units can earn the First Phase label once the host country files its BTR, or earlier through insurance. Because countries file BTRs only every two years, insurance is often the only route to credits becoming eligible. Insurers price their cover on the same readiness factors, so where they won't cover a country, its volumes may have to wait for the next reporting cycle.


The third is how commercially workable a government's rules are. Some countries require developers to use national registries, most of which aren't ICAO-approved. Developers that move credits into them may lose CORSIA eligibility. Some governments charge corresponding adjustment fees of up to $5 per tonne, occasionally upfront. With spot prices at $12 to $13, a fee of that size can make a project uneconomical.


The fourth, cost competitiveness, follows from the rest. Developers need projects that can absorb a price that has swung from above $20 to around $9 and back up to $13.


## Host governments need the economic case, and better coordination


Authorising units for CORSIA asks a lot from governments. They give up emissions reductions that would otherwise count towards their own climate targets, so they need to see a clear return.


That was the starting point for the[ASEAN CORSIA market report](https://abatable.com/reports/unlocking-the-billion-dollar-corsia-potential-in-asean) Abatable co-authored with Boeing and GenZero in June. We set out to show governments the economic opportunity that sits alongside the trade-offs they already weigh. At the time, we estimated the potential pool of CEEUs across ASEAN at 133mn to 302mn units, worth $1.6bn to $8.5bn, an amount capable of supporting around 32,000 new jobs.


The numbers have moved since June. Eligible supply from ASEAN has roughly doubled, from 2.6mn to 5.4mn units, across seven cookstove projects in Cambodia and Laos. Units from projects using CORSIA-aligned methodologies, but which are not yet authorised, have risen 62%, from 18.2mn to 27.8mn. Vietnam accounts for 14.7mn of those, and Laos has a jurisdictional REDD+ programme in the mix.


Abatable’s conversations with governments have surfaced recurring concerns: the risk of overselling and missing NDC targets, poor visibility of the project pipeline, and limited coordination between ministries. Inter-ministerial committees set up to handle Article 6 sometimes left CORSIA out of their thinking altogether. The report recommends cross-ministerial coordination bodies, clear lists of eligible sectors and project types, and mapping potential CORSIA supply against NDC commitments.


In the webinar, Kevin Lee from IATA highlighted a related gap. Specialists in Article 6 and aviation often don't know what the other side needs, and the CORSIA and Paris Agreement reporting timelines don't line up. Sharmine Tan from Boeing outlined that the company is running workshops with the environment ministries that own each country's NDC to help close that knowledge gap.


## Airlines are building procurement capability


Many airlines spent the early part of this year waiting to see how the market would settle. That's changing, and the early movers are now using their first purchases to build the internal capability they'll need for larger obligations.


Malaysia Aviation Group is one of them. As Azfar Mohamed Bin Ameer Abdullah, from the company’s sustainability office, outlined, it treats CORSIA as one of four levers in its new mid-term sustainability roadmap, which was launched the week before the webinar. Fleet renewal comes first, with new-generation aircraft using around 15% less fuel. Operational efficiency measures saved about 30,000 tonnes of jet fuel in 2025, equating to roughly 100,000 tonnes of CO₂. The group already uses Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) on flights departing the EU and UK under those mandates. CORSIA units then cover residual emissions while those in-sector measures scale up.


The group has retired around 80,000 CEEUs through a pilot procurement programme, and its lessons echo those from other airlines. Buying carbon credits is more complex than buying most commodities. CORSIA often sits with the sustainability team, but a purchase needs finance, treasury, legal, and procurement colleagues too, and annual procurement cycles rarely match the timing of unit availability. A small pilot lets an airline test its governance, approval, retirement, and reporting processes with limited money at stake.


Airlines also need to plan around limited supply. Malaysia Aviation Group is diversifying by project type and geography to manage delivery risk, and our report[recommends](https://abatable.com/reports/unlocking-the-billion-dollar-corsia-potential-in-asean) airlines consider forward purchases alongside spot deals. Budgets are tight too. Boeing’s Sharmine Tan pointed out that airlines work on thin margins and weigh every dollar spent on CEEUs against the same dollar spent on SAF.


## Deals depend on sharing risk and information


In a compliance market like CORSIA, buyers want the cheapest unit that arrives on time and to specification. Minh Tran from Bridge Carbon described how far apart buyers and sellers can start. Some airlines will only buy fully labelled units on a spot basis, with the seller carrying every risk. Developers face several possible failure points before a unit is labelled, and most lack the balance sheet to offer large financial guarantees. Traders have stepped in to lend theirs, which keeps transactions moving.


Participants began with standardised contract structures borrowed from markets such as LNG and crude oil, and have since moved to more bespoke terms on pricing, delivery, and guarantees. Bridge Carbon's advice to everyone in the market is to work out which risks they can absorb and control, which they can't, and then agree on a balanced split.


Buyers and sellers also want more information from each other. As Azfar Mohamed Bin Ameer Abdullah outlined, Malaysia Aviation Group wants greater certainty of supply, more eligible units from ASEAN projects, and clearer insight into pricing. It currently has little visibility of how corresponding adjustment fees and insurance premiums feed into the cost of each unit.


Developers want clear demand signals in return. As Tran stated, Bridge Carbon has already deployed capital to bring volumes online and needs to know which airlines plan to buy, when, and in what quantity. Each side holds information the other needs to plan, and the sooner they share it, the sooner the market can match supply to demand.


## Working together before the deadline


As Kevin Lee stated, IATA has responded to these challenges by bringing industry actors together. Its supporting alliance, built around the Aviation Carbon Markets Compact, asks each signatory to commit to a specific action: airlines to buy CEEUs, developers to bring supply to market, and others to play their own part. More than 80 organisations have signed, including Abatable, Malaysia Aviation Group, and Boeing, and the alliance now offers implementation support to host countries.


This joint approach reflects the clearest takeaway from the webinar. No single group can close the First Phase supply gap on its own. Governments that publish clear authorisation policies and coordinate across ministries give developers the certainty to invest. Airlines that signal their volumes and run pilot purchases now will find larger procurements easier. Developers, insurers, and traders who share risk sensibly will get more deals over the line.


CORSIA took a decade to reach its first real compliance cycle. How much of the 200mn-unit First Phase requirement airlines can meet with high-quality supply now rests on how quickly each of those groups acts on what it has learned this year.


## Your questions answered


We received more questions in the webinar than we had time to answer. Here are our responses to some of the most common, covering pricing, guarantees, CORSIA's interaction with the EU Emissions Trading System, and enforcement.


### How does CORSIA interact with the EU ETS?


The two schemes consider Europe's aviation emissions by route. The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) covers flights within the European Economic Area (EEA), and from the EEA to the UK and Switzerland; these are considered intra-Europe. Any extra-European flight is not covered by the EU-ETS. On the side of CORSIA, any international flight where the origin and destination are in two different countries, both participating, become a CORSIA route and so the flight is subject to offsetting requirements. In that sense, both intra-European and extra-European flights between distinct countries would be subject to CORSIA.


The interaction between both schemes comes down to how participating airlines demonstrate compliance. Under CORSIA, they must purchase and retire CEEUs in an amount equivalent to their emissions growth during each of the three-year compliance cycles if exceeding the emissions baseline. Under the EU-ETS, participating airlines must surrender emissions allowances in a quantity that covers their annual emissions.


That split may change. In July 2026, the European Commission proposed keeping CORSIA for most international flights to 2035, while extending the EU ETS from 2029 to departures for destinations within a 5,000 km radius of Frankfurt airport. On those routes, the EU ETS would act as a top-up: airlines' ETS obligations would be reduced to reflect what they've already paid under CORSIA, so they aren't charged twice. The Commission plans to review CORSIA again in 2032. The proposal still needs agreement from the European Parliament and member states, so the final rules may differ.


### Does the 200mn tonne phase one estimate account for intra-EU flights falling under the EU ETS?


Yes. Abatable's modelling includes flights within the EEA as per ICAO rules, and published data on emissions subject to offsetting requirements. The 200mn tonne figure reflects the international routes where airlines face CORSIA offsetting requirements for all pairs of countries participating in each phase. It's also broadly in line with ICAO's own estimate of around 200mn tonnes for the first phase.


### Is today's $12 to $13 price a reliable guide for forward supply?


Airlines have retired just over one million units against First Phase demand of around 200mn, so today's price reflects a small number of early trades on limited labelled supply. Most of the buying has yet to happen, and the prices may change.


Several factors could impact price as the CORSIA First Phase deadline nears. Labelled supply today stands at around 55mn tonnes, short of demand, and several of our panellists expect that gap to push prices up. Developers' costs matter too: corresponding adjustment fees, insurance premiums, and the time host countries take to issue authorisations all feed into what new supply costs to bring to market. And the price has already swung from above $20 to around $9 and back to $12 to $13 in a short period. The prices reflected on indices for future deliveries have higher prices for the delivery months closer to the compliance deadline.


Today's price is a useful reference for spot deals. Forward contracts need to reflect delivery risk and timing as well, and we expect buyers and sellers to use a mix of fixed and floating pricing to share that risk.


### What's the difference between CORSIA-eligible and CORSIA-aligned units?


CORSIA-eligible units are ready for airlines to use. They come from an ICAO-approved programme such as Verra, Gold Standard, ACR or ART, and meet ICAO’s First Phase eligibility criteria: a first crediting period starting on or after 1 January 2016, use of allowed methodologies and activity types, and reductions that occurred between 2021 and 2026. These units also carry the host country's LoA, indicating their use for CORSIA, and are backed by assurance against double claiming through the country's reporting or an approved insurance policy. When a unit covers all these characteristics, then it can become labelled as CORSIA-eligible in the registry of the carbon crediting standard or programme.


CORSIA-aligned units meet the programme, methodology, and vintage criteria but don't yet have an LoA, and do not hold a guarantee for the avoidance of double counting, so airlines can't use them for compliance as the units are not labelled yet in the registry. They're potential supply: once the host country authorises them and the guarantees are confirmed, they can become eligible. In ASEAN alone, around 27.8mn aligned units are waiting on that step, compared with 5.4mn eligible units.


### What's the biggest barrier preventing the CORSIA market from scaling up to meet airlines' demand?


Host government authorisation is a significant factor. Developers have projects ready, in many cases with issued units, and capital deployed, but their units can't become eligible until the host country issues a letter of authorisation and can credibly deliver the corresponding adjustment. This requires a national framework that gives the letter legal force, an authorised volume that fits the country's NDC, and the capacity to report on time. Insurers price their cover on the same factors, so a country that falls short on readiness can hold back supply even after issuing letters.


Governments face real trade-offs, because each tonne they authorise no longer counts towards their own climate target. Clear authorisation policies, coordination between environment and transport ministries, and proportionate corresponding adjustment fees would help bring more supply forward. Airlines can help too, by signalling when and how much they plan to buy so developers and governments can plan with confidence.
